2	name: horizon
3	description: How to work inside an Archon Horizon workspace — orient from on-disk state, pick the highest-value formalization work, record progress as commits, and coordinate. Load this first; it points to the specialized skills for detail. Editable per workspace.
4	---
5	
6	You are working inside an **Archon Horizon** workspace: a place where AI agents
7	formalize mathematics in Lean 4 across one or more projects. This skill is the
8	map. It is deliberately short and **you can edit it** (it lives at
9	`.claude/skills/horizon/SKILL.md` in this workspace) — tune it to how you want to
10	work. It points to focused skills; load those on demand rather than up front.
11	
12	## You are a team; the workspace is where teams collaborate
13	
14	Think of your session as **one team**: you (the lead) plus the subagents you
15	spawn as your **workers**, with the tools and skills available to you. A
16	`horizon run` is your team working through its task. Other runs are **other
17	teams** working in parallel on the *same shared workspace* — one Lean project set,
18	one roadmap/board, one ledger, one inbox.
19	
20	You do not manage other teams and they do not manage you. You coordinate through
21	**shared state**, not meetings:
22	
23	- **The board (roadmap)** is the shared plan. Keep your items' status/owner/
24	  milestone current so other teams see what you hold and where it's going.
25	- **The inbox** is asynchronous messaging + memory across teams (skill:
26	  `horizon-inbox`): shared notes, per-task private items, and direct messages to
27	  another team.
28	- **Commits** are the durable record; reading recent ledger history tells you what
29	  other teams just produced (skill: `project-git`).
30	
31	Before you start, be aware of who else is live (see "Is another run live" below).
32	A short **synchronizer** digest is printed to stderr at the start of your CLI
33	commands (unread inbox for your task, your session's runtime/tokens, other live
34	runs) — read it; it is how you stay aware without asking anyone.
35	
36	## Orient (pull state, don't assume it)
37	
38	**Start here:** your prompt says nothing about who ran before you. Usually
39	somebody did — often minutes ago, often on this same task, and their report was
40	written for you. Skill: `horizon-start` — one cheap pass that works out which
41	situation you were launched into (fresh run, hand-off from the session that just
42	finished, resume after a crash, or outside a run) and what to read for each.
43	
44	The workspace root is `$ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT`; your shell may start in a member
45	project rather than at that root. The absolute path to this skill is
46	`$ARCHON_HORIZON_SKILL`. Live state is under
47	`$ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT/.archon-horizon/` and the manifest is
48	`$ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT/config.yaml`. Read what you need, when you need it — via the
49	`horizon` CLI (invoke it as `"$HORIZON_BIN" …`):
50	
51	- **Roadmap** — YOUR strategy sketch across *all* projects, kept as a nested
52	  outline. `"$HORIZON_BIN" roadmap list` renders the indented tree with per-parent
53	  progress (`active · 3/7 done`); `--focus <id>` shows one subtree, `--max-depth 0`
54	  the top level only. Structure it: nest sub-goals with `--parent`, keep your
55	  item's status/strategy current as you work. It doubles as the **project board**:
56	  set `--owner <team>` (who holds it), `--milestone <label>` (a free grouping tag,
57	  filter with `roadmap list --milestone <label>`), and pin concrete deliverables
58	  with `--pin-commit <sha>`. Roadmap commands print a **warning**
59	  when parent/child statuses disagree (all sub-items done but parent open, or a
60	  done parent with open children) — nothing is auto-corrected; you decide whether
61	  to fix it or leave it (it may be intentional). They also warn when too many
62	  milestones claim simultaneous `active` focus.
63	- **Tasks** — a specific piece of work, usually the one a human launched and is
64	  watching. `"$HORIZON_BIN" task …`. Task commands warn when the open queue grows
65	  beyond the advisory limit or a `running` status looks orphaned.

68	  `horizon-inbox`). Items can be **owned by your task** (private, e.g. your team's

101	## Pace yourself (usage & interruption risk)
102	
103	Sessions end for reasons you don't control: rate limits, usage caps, budgets.
104	The defense is NOT to avoid work — it is to make interruption cheap:
105	
106	- **Commit at every coherent point** (plain git into the ledger, below). If
107	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" usage --json` shows low budget headroom or recent
108	  `rate_limit`/`usage_limit` signals, commit what you have NOW and prefer
109	  finishing the piece in flight over opening a new front.

112	  the roadmap/task status, and write the report as if nobody continues today.
113	- Interrupted anyway? Nothing is lost that was committed — the next session
114	  resumes from the ledger (see "Resuming" below).

116	## One-shot discipline (important)
117	
118	This session runs to completion and is **not resumed** — you will not be re-invoked
119	when a background job finishes. So **run work in the foreground and block on it**
120	(builds, checks, subagents). Anything you leave running in the background, or leave
121	uncommitted, may be lost when the session ends. Commit early and often (below).
122	
123	## Pick the highest-value work
124	
125	Read the roadmap and the live Lean state, then commit to the most valuable next
126	piece. A node being large, multi-session, or blocked on missing mathlib
127	infrastructure is **not** a reason to skip it — start it, build the missing
128	lemma/definition yourself as project-local infrastructure, and push it as far as
129	you genuinely can. Prefer ambitious progress over defensive avoidance.
130	
131	If this session was launched on a specific task, make concrete progress on that
132	task's REAL objective — don't preemptively pivot to easy unrelated wins because
133	the objective is large. Leave a `"$HORIZON_BIN" task comment <task_id> --body …`
134	at each significant step. You own the task's terminal status (skill:
135	`task-status`): set `--status done` only when the objective is FULLY complete;

141	The old Ground pass is no longer a second orchestrator role, but independent

144	
145	- before marking a multi-step task `done`;

264	staging explicit files over `add -A`. Beyond commits:
265	
266	- Update the **roadmap** with coarse status/strategy (not a re-narration of the diff).
267	- Use the **inbox** to hand off to the next/other sessions; record durable dead-ends
268	  as **memory**.
269	
270	Before your final report, do one boundary-maintenance pass. Re-read the task's
271	`roadmap_refs` and `inbox_refs`; update each roadmap milestone whose status or
272	strategy changed, add a concise mathematical comment for a key advance, and
273	archive or complete open inbox items your work actually resolved. Also scan the
274	remaining open inbox for consumed temporary/info/memory items and archive those
275	that are now stale. Never archive a standing protection merely to make the list
276	shorter. This pass is part of completing the work, not optional janitor follow-up.
277	
278	## Resuming after an interruption
279	
280	State lives on disk, so a fresh session (even on another account) continues
281	cheaply. Working out *whether* you're resuming, and what to read if you are, is
282	the `horizon-start` skill — load it at the start of the session. The essentials:
283	
284	- **Why did the last run stop?** `"$HORIZON_BIN" usage --json` includes a
285	  `paused` field (from `runs/<id>/paused.json`) with the reason (usage limit,
286	  budget, …) and the exact resume command; `recent_failure_reasons` shows
287	  rate-limit signals. A paused/killed run resumes with
288	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" run --resume <id>`.
289	- **What was in flight?** Read recent ledger history (`project-git` skill:
290	  `git log` + `git show` by `Archon-Session` trailer) and the previous
291	  session's transcript/report under `.archon-horizon/runs/`. A horizon session
292	  directory with **no `report.md`** is one that was killed mid-flight.
293	- **Is another run live on this workspace?** `"$HORIZON_BIN" ps` lists runs
294	  holding a process (the ledger is one shared branch — be aware of parallel
295	  writers); it also flags zombie markers and stalled runs. A run registers a
296	  `runs/<id>/process.json` marker (pid/host) at start and removes it on clean
297	  exit; `ps` decides liveness by probing the pid on the local host (a marker whose
298	  pid is dead is a reap-able zombie, a live pid idle for a long time is "stalled").
299	  The synchronizer surfaces the same "other runs live" signal at command start, so
300	  you usually don't need to call `ps` explicitly.
301	
302	## Final report (your last message)
303	
304	Your final message is saved as the session's report — a human or the next
305	session should understand the session from it without opening raw logs.
306	Recommended sections: `## Summary`, `## Progress`, `## Issues`,
307	`## Why I stopped`, `## Next` (keep at least `## Progress` and
308	`## Why I stopped`). In `## Progress`, one inline `-` bullet per file/target,
309	e.g. `- FileA.lean: 4 sorries -> 3; closed the base case.` In `## Why I
310	stopped`, say plainly whether the objective is fully complete, partly advanced,
311	or blocked — and why. Always mention build failures, broken proofs, blocked
312	dependencies, and checks that failed or were not run. If a plausible next
313	action fits in the session's scope, take it before stopping — a clean commit is
314	not by itself a reason to stop.
315	
316	## Cleaning up the work (you decide, via subagents)
317	
318	There is no second orchestrator role running alongside you. *You* are the driver,
319	and the **`ground`** subagent is the scheduled fresh-context checkpoint when the
320	workspace or strategy needs an external view. Available helpers (see the
321	`subagents` skill):
322	
323	- **janitor** — workspace hygiene: roadmap/READMEs concise, inbox from overflowing.
324	- **ground** — workspace-wide strategy, graph, ledger, and convergence review.
325	- **work-reviewer** — fresh-context review of your last work; is it converging?
326	- **blueprint** — Lean ↔ blueprint statement/`\uses` correctness for a scoped slice.
327	- **reference-retriever**, **debug**, **page-transcriber** — as needed.
328	
329	Keep proving; delegate the upkeep.

\chapter{FGA representability of the Picard scheme}
\label{chap:Picard_FGAPicRepresentability}
% archon:covers AlgebraicJacobian/Picard/FGAPicRepresentability.lean

\section{Setup and motivation}
\label{sec:fga_pic_setup}

Throughout this chapter, fix a base field \(k\) and a smooth proper geometrically
integral curve \(C\) over \(k\) (the curve carrying the Jacobian). The relative
Picard presheaf \(\Pic^\sharp_{C/k} : (\Sch/k)^{op} \to \Set\) of
\cref{chap:Picard_LineBundlePullback} has already been packaged as a
set-valued functor and refined to its abelian-group-valued
\'etale-sheafified version \(\Pic^\sharp_{(C/k)\et}\) in
\cref{chap:Picard_RelPicFunctor}. The Quot scheme machinery of
\cref{chap:Picard_QuotScheme} supplies the representing engine: for
\(C/k\) projective and flat with integral geometric fibers, the Hilbert scheme
\(\Hilb_{C/k}\) and its open subscheme \(\mathrm{Div}_{C/k}\) of relative effective
divisors are both representable by quasi-projective \(k\)-schemes. Grothendieck's
existence theorem for \(\Pic\) assembles these two ingredients via the Abel
map \(\mathrm{Div}_{C/k} \to \Pic^\sharp_{C/k}\) to produce a representing scheme,
the \emph{Picard scheme} \(\Pic_{C/k}\). The present chapter packages this
assembly: a line-bundle / Quot correspondence, the FGA representability
theorem, and the abelian-group-scheme refinement.

\medskip

\textbf{Comparison with the sheafified Picard functor.} Kleiman \S 4 represents
the \'etale-sheafified functor \(\Pic_{(C/k)\et}\). This chapter instead
works throughout under the standing hypothesis that \emph{\(C\) has a
\(k\)-rational point} (\cref{def:has_rational_point}) and states
representability against the \emph{plain} relative Picard functor
\(\Pic^\sharp_{C/k}\) of \cref{def:rel_pic_sharp}. This is justified by
Kleiman \S 2, Thm.~2.5 (\texttt{th:comp}): if \(f : X \to S\) has a section
and \(\mathcal O_{S'} = f'_* \mathcal O_{X'}\) holds for all base changes
(automatic for our proper geometrically integral curve, by cohomology and
base change), then the comparison maps
\[
  \Pic_{X/S}(T) \longrightarrow \Pic_{(X/S)\et}(T) \longrightarrow
  \Pic_{(X/S)\fppf}(T)
\]
are bijective for every \(T\). Hence under the rational-point hypothesis the
plain relative functor \emph{is} the \'etale sheaf, so the rational point
allows us to work directly with \(\Pic^\sharp_{C/k}\).
Without a section the plain functor is not even a Zariski sheaf in
general, so every representability assertion of this chapter carries the
rational-point hypothesis. A pointed curve \((C,P)\), as in
\cref{chap:AbelJacobi}, supplies such a section.

% SOURCE: [Kleiman], ``The Picard scheme'', \S 4 (FGA Explained Ch.~9 \S 9.4);
% arXiv:math/0504020, p.~26. Read from
% references/kleiman-picard-src/kleiman-picard.tex.

\section{Line bundles and the Quot / Hilbert scheme}
\label{sec:fga_pic_line_bundle_quot}

The bridge from line bundles on \(C \times_k T\) to the Quot scheme is the
Abel map: a relative effective divisor \(D \subset C \times_k T\) over \(T\)
(a \(T\)-flat closed subscheme whose ideal is invertible) determines a closed
subscheme of \(C \times_k T\) flat over \(T\), hence a \(T\)-point of the Hilbert
functor \(\Hilb_{C/k}(T)\), which is the special case \(\Quot_{\mathcal{O}_C/C/k}\)

\section{The FGA representability theorem}
\label{sec:fga_pic_representability}

We now state and prove the specialisation of Grothendieck's existence theorem
for the Picard scheme, in the specialisation needed for the Jacobian:
\(S = \Spec k\), \(X = C\) a smooth proper geometrically integral
curve. The general theorem (Kleiman \S 4, Thm.~4.8) covers any
\(X/S\) projective Zariski-locally over \(S\), flat, with integral geometric
fibers; we record the general statement and then specialise.

\begin{theorem}[FGA representability of the Picard scheme]\leanok
  \label{thm:fga_pic_representability}
  \lean{AlgebraicGeometry.Scheme.PicScheme.representable}
  \uses{lem:line_bundle_quot_correspondence, lem:smooth_proper_quotient,
        thm:quot_representable, def:rel_pic_sharp, def:has_rational_point,
        cor:flattening_stratification_curve, def:pic_sharp_representable,
        def:inst_pic_sharp_representable, lem:cech_flat_base_change}
  % SOURCE: [Kleiman], ``The Picard scheme'', \S 4, Main Thm.~th:main,
  % and Cor.~cor:algsch (specialisation to \(S = \Spec k\), \(X\) complete);
  % arXiv:math/0504020, pp.~26, 35 (read from
  % references/kleiman-picard-src/kleiman-picard.tex, L2155-L2166 + L2686-L2690).
  % Source identifiers: \begin{thm}\label{th:main}\end{thm}
  % and \begin{sbscor}\label{cor:algsch}\end{sbscor}.
  \textit{Source: [Kleiman], ``The Picard scheme'', \S 4, Main Thm.~4.8
  + Cor.~4.18.3.}
  Let \(k\) be a field and \(C\) a smooth proper geometrically integral curve
  over \(k\) \emph{with a \(k\)-rational point}
  (\cref{def:has_rational_point}). Then the relative Picard functor
  \(\Pic^\sharp_{C/k}\) of \cref{def:rel_pic_sharp} --- which under the
  rational-point hypothesis coincides with its \'etale sheafification
  \(\Pic_{(C/k)\et}\), by Kleiman \S 2, Thm.~2.5 --- is representable by a
  \(k\)-scheme \(\Pic_{C/k}\), separated and locally of finite type over
  \(k\), which is a disjoint union of open quasi-projective
  \(k\)-subschemes, each an increasing union of open quasi-projective
  subschemes. The scheme \(\Pic_{C/k}\) is called the \emph{Picard scheme}
  of \(C/k\).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
  
  We follow Kleiman~\S 4, Thm.~4.8, specialised to \(S = \Spec k\) and
  \(X = C\). The proof proceeds in four conceptual steps, preceded by a
  comparison step; the underlying algebraic engine is the Quot scheme of
  \cref{chap:Picard_QuotScheme} and the relative Picard functor of
  \cref{chap:Picard_RelPicFunctor}, together with the line-bundle / Quot
  correspondence of \cref{lem:line_bundle_quot_correspondence}.

  \emph{Step 0: reduce to the \'etale sheaf via the rational point.}
  By Kleiman \S 2, Thm.~2.5, since \(C \to \Spec k\) has a section
  (\cref{def:has_rational_point}) and \(\mathcal O_T = \pi_{T*}
  \mathcal O_{C \times_k T}\) holds for every \(k\)-scheme \(T\) (cohomology
  and base change for the proper geometrically integral fibers of
  \(C\times_k T/T\)), the comparison map
  \(\Pic^\sharp_{C/k}(T) \to \Pic_{(C/k)\et}(T)\) is bijective for all
  \(T\). It therefore suffices to represent the \'etale sheaf
  \(\Pic_{(C/k)\et}\), which is what Kleiman's theorem produces; the same
  scheme then represents \(\Pic^\sharp_{C/k}\).

  \emph{Step 1: stratify by Hilbert polynomial.}
  For each polynomial \(\phi \in \mathbb{Q}[n]\), let \(P^\phi \subseteq
  \Pic^\sharp_{(C/k)\et}\) be the \'etale subsheaf whose \(T\)-points are
  represented by invertible sheaves \(\mathcal{L}\) on \(C \times_k T\) with
  \(\chi(C_t, \mathcal{L}_t^{-1}(n)) = \phi(n)\) for all \(t \in T\) (the
  Hilbert polynomial relative to the chosen polarisation
  \(\mathcal{O}_C(1)\) on the projective curve \(C\)). The \(P^\phi\) form a
  disjoint open cover of \(\Pic^\sharp_{(C/k)\et}\) (openness via Kleiman's
  flat-base-change argument, \cref{lem:cech_flat_base_change} / Stacks Tag 02KH;
  cf.\ EGA III 7.9.11). It suffices to
  represent each \(P^\phi\) by an increasing union of open quasi-projective
  \(k\)-schemes.

  \emph{Step 2: bound twists by \(m\)-regularity.}
  Given \(\phi\), fix \(m\) large enough that the \(T\)-points of \(P^\phi\) are
  representable by \(\mathcal{L}\) on \(C \times_k T\) satisfying
  \(R^i \pi_{T*} \mathcal{L}(n) = 0\) for all \(i \ge 1\), \(n \ge m\). Twisting
  by \(\mathcal{O}_C(m)\) defines an automorphism of \(\Pic^\sharp_{(C/k)\et}\)
  that carries \(P^\phi\) to \(P^{\phi_0}_0\) for \(\phi_0(n) := \phi(m + n)\).
  Hence it suffices to represent each \(P^{\phi_0}_0\) by a quasi-projective
  \(k\)-scheme.

  \emph{Step 3: factor through the Abel map.}
  Consider the Abel map \(A_{C/k} : \mathrm{Div}_{C/k} \to \Pic^\sharp_{(C/k)\et}\)
  of \cref{lem:line_bundle_quot_correspondence}. The source \(\mathrm{Div}_{C/k}\)

  of an equivalence relation on \(Z\), hence injective on \(T\)-points).
  By EGA IV 8.11.5, a proper monomorphism is a closed immersion: \(h\) is a
  closed embedding.

  Hence \(R \hookrightarrow Z \times_k Z\) is a flat (by (iv)) and proper
  equivalence relation on the quasi-projective \(k\)-scheme \(Z\). By the
  theory of flat-and-proper effective equivalence relations on
  quasi-projective schemes (Altman--Kleiman; the construction places
  the graph \(R \subseteq Z \times_k Z\) inside the universal subscheme of
  the Hilbert scheme \(\Hilb_{Z/k}\) and descends to a closed subscheme

  quasi-projective \(k\)-scheme \(Q\) and a faithfully flat, projective map

  The map \(Z \to Q\) is flat and proper; its fibers, up to field
  extension, coincide with those of \(R \to Z\), which are smooth by

  Finally, \(Z \to Q\) is a surjection of \'etale sheaves (an \'etale

  isomorphism, so \(Q\) represents \(P\). Smoothness of \(\alpha : Z \to P\)

    [SmoothOfRelativeDimension 1 C.hom] [IsProper C.hom]
    [GeometricallyIntegral C.hom] [HasPicScheme C] : Prop where
  has_representable : Nonempty ((picSharp C).RepresentableBy (PicScheme C))

/-- Existence instance for `PicSharpRepresentable`: `PicScheme C` is
`Classical.choose` of the `HasPicScheme` existential, and the first component
of `Exists.choose_spec` says precisely that the chosen scheme represents
`picSharp C` (the remaining components are local finiteness and
separatedness). The FGA content lives upstream in `instHasPicScheme`. -/
instance instPicSharpRepresentable {k : Type u} [Field k]
    (C : Over (Spec (.of k)))
    [SmoothOfRelativeDimension 1 C.hom] [IsProper C.hom]
    [GeometricallyIntegral C.hom] [HasPicScheme C] : PicSharpRepresentable C :=
  ⟨(HasPicScheme.has_pic_scheme (C := C)).choose_spec.1⟩

/-- **FGA representability of the Picard scheme.**

Let `k` be a field and `C` a smooth proper geometrically integral curve over
`k` (with, through the `HasPicScheme` hypothesis chain, a `k`-rational
point). Then the relative Picard functor `Pic^♯_{C/k}` is representable by
the Picard scheme `PicScheme C`: there is a natural bijection

```
(T ⟶ Pic_{C/k}) ≃ Pic(C ×_k T)/π_T^* Pic(T)
```

for every `k`-scheme `T`. This `RepresentableBy` structure is a comparison
against the relative Picard functor itself, so downstream consumers
(tangent-space computation at the identity, `Pic⁰` degree theory) can compose
with its `homEquiv` to transfer line-bundle data to scheme points. -/

\textbf{Two routes to representability.} The Picard scheme of a curve can be
constructed in two ways, and this blueprint records both, because they need
different inputs and only one of them is the route under construction here.

The \emph{quotient route} is Grothendieck's, as presented by Kleiman \S 4: the
Abel map \(\mathrm{Div}_{C/k} \to \Pic^\sharp_{C/k}\) exhibits the Picard functor
as a quotient of a quasi-projective scheme by a smooth proper equivalence
relation, and Altman--Kleiman descent
(\cref{lem:smooth_proper_quotient}) represents the quotient. Its engine is the
Hilbert scheme \(\Hilb_{C/k} = \Quot_{\mathcal{O}_C/C/k}\) of
\cref{chap:Picard_QuotScheme}, whose open subscheme \(\mathrm{Div}_{C/k}\) of
relative effective divisors carries the source of the Abel map. This is the route
of \cref{thm:fga_pic_representability} and its proof below.

The \emph{Milne--Koll\'ar route} builds \(\Pic^r_{C/k}\) directly, over a
separably closed field, from the open loci
\[
  C^\Sigma = \{\,t : h^0(\mathcal{O}(W - \Sigma)_t) = 1\,\}
\]
cut out inside a degree-\(r\) divisor scheme by a tuple \(\Sigma\) of rational
points, glues them, and descends the result to \(k\) by a finite Galois quotient
before assembling the degrees by a coproduct. Its inputs are a rigidified
pushforward engine, uniform \(H^1\) vanishing, and Galois descent of rigidified
classes --- not a Hilbert or Quot scheme.

The decisive difference is the quotient step. Altman--Kleiman descent needs
quasi-projectivity of the scheme being quotiented, which is not expressible in
the formalisation at present and without which the lemma is false
(\cref{rem:smooth_proper_quotient_hypothesis}); the Milne--Koll\'ar route takes
only finite Galois quotients under an orbit-in-affine hypothesis, and so avoids
that obstruction entirely. The Lean development therefore pursues the
Milne--Koll\'ar route. The quotient-route material below is retained as the
mathematics it is --- the divisor and Hilbert-scheme substrate it rests on is
consumed by both routes --- and is not the path currently being formalised.
